hook_text: People say from here to Timbuktu to mean the middle of nowhere. But Timbuktu was once the middle of everything.
clip_script: Picture the edge of the Sahara, where the Niger River curves up into the desert. Camels arrive from the north, loaded with salt, cloth and books. Boats arrive from the south, loaded with gold and kola nuts. Camels can't survive in the wet south. Boats can't cross the sand. So everything changes hands right here: Timbuktu, the port of the desert. Around 1510 a young traveller from Morocco walked its streets and later wrote it all down: weavers, merchants, a king with plates of gold, and markets where books sold for more profit than anything else. His name was Leo Africanus. He wrote years later, in Rome, for European readers, so historians check his story. But it is clear: Timbuktu was no myth.
visual_style: A whiteboard map zooming into the Niger bend; camel icons arriving from the top, boat icons from below, meeting at a city dot; an open book with Description of Africa 1550 on the cover.
